title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
claim: Generation attends mainly to moving regions while static regions stay highly similar across frames, revealing exploitable redundancy for sparse computation.
layout: 2 columns by 3 stacked rows, top-to-bottom, film-strip frames, heatmap overlays
description: The figure has two side-by-side columns separated by a dashed vertical line. Each column starts with a text prompt: a smooth countryside landscape shot on the left (camera panning) and a stylish woman walking down a Tokyo street on the right (subject motion). Each column has three stacked rows of three consecutive frames. Row (a) shows the generated real-world frames in a black film-strip border. Row (b) shows attention distribution heatmaps overlaid on the frames, with bright green and cyan highlighting the moving road or the woman against a purple background. Row (c) shows cosine-similarity maps in mostly red, where static areas are uniformly high and blue or yellow edges mark dynamic regions. The eye goes first to the colorful film strips, then to the heatmaps.
caption: Spatiotemporal dynamic analysis of video generation under different motion priors (left: camera panning; right: subject motion). (a) Real-world scenes. The videos are synthesized via Self Forcing, conditioned on a single text prompt provided at the initialization stage. (b) Attention distributions. Visualizations reveal the distribution of temporal attention scores, indicating that the generation process predominantly focuses on active dynamic elements alongside adjacent temporal context. (c) Cosine similarity between the currently generated frame and preceding frames. The consistently high similarity observed in static background regions demonstrates the potential for extensive feature reuse during computation.
abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
